conclusion: Two copies of the common C allele at SIRT6 rs117385980 - the usual result, carried by roughly 95-96% of people. In the only two cohorts that have examined this variant, individuals who had reached the oldest ages were more often C/C, but neither study reached statistical significance (p = 0.074 in 198 Finnish men; p = 0.073 across age bands in 227 Iranian adults). Treat this as a direction of trend, not an established finding. Nothing about medical care or lifestyle follows from this genotype.
phenotype: Longevity / survival to advanced age; frailty (Fried phenotype)

conclusion: One copy of the rarer T allele at SIRT6 rs117385980; about 4% of people carry it (3.6-4.5%, depending on the gnomAD subset). Two small studies - 198 Finnish men and 227 Iranian adults aged 60-90 - both found T carriers under-represented among their oldest participants, and in both the result fell short of significance (OR 3.58, 95% CI 0.96-13.4, p = 0.074 for being in the shorter-lived group; and 0 of 40 carriers at ages 80-90 versus 1.4-4.7% at younger ages, p = 0.073). The Iranian study's own primary question - frailty - came out null (adjusted OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.10-9.66, p = 0.98). The entire world literature on this variant rests on fewer than 20 heterozygotes. This is a weak same-direction trend across two cohorts, not an established effect, and it is not a basis for any health decision.
negatives: Counterpart worth stating: in the Iranian cohort the T allele was numerically MORE common among robust (non-frail) participants (2.1% of non-frail alleles versus 0% of frail), which points the opposite way to the survival trend. The authors read the pair as a possible antagonistic pleiotropy - an allele that is neutral or mildly favourable earlier in life and disadvantageous at the oldest ages. Both halves are non-significant and the frail group contributed only 78 alleles, so chance alone explains the 0%.
phenotype: Longevity / survival to advanced age; frailty (Fried phenotype)

conclusion: Two copies of the T allele at SIRT6 rs117385980. No published study of frailty or longevity has reported a single T/T individual - not one among the 425 people in the two cohorts that have genotyped this variant - so there is no evidence at all about what this genotype means for ageing or survival. The genotype is nonetheless real and not vanishingly rare: gnomAD v4 records 183 T/T individuals among roughly 287,000 sequenced people, which is also the strongest single argument that this variant is not the protein-truncating change it has been described as (see README). Absence of data is not evidence of harm, nor of benefit.
